newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs clash over plans to patent human material.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs clash over plans to patent human material.

text.p: European Parliament deputies clashed on Tuesday in the latest round of a nine-year quest to agree Europe-wide rules on patents for biotechological inventions using living material, including genetic engineering.

After vetoing in 1995 a draft patent law approved by European Union governments, Euro-MPs tried on Tuesday to come to terms with a new proposal from the European Commission -- amidst heavy lobbying by industrial, environmental and medical groups.

The Commission told Euro-deputies the new proposal sought to quell their earlier concerns about the ethical consequences of allowing industrial companies to own living human, animal or plant material.

Single Market Commissioner Mario Monti said it had tried clearly to distinguish between discoveries of elements that already existed in nature -- which could never be patented -- and inventions using this basic biological material to solve particular problems. But deputies, who will vote on the proposal on Wednesday, have proposed more than 100 amendments to tighten up the text. The proposal then goes to EU ministers before returning to the parliament for a final assessment.

The Commission and industry argue that companies should be able to patent inventions using human material to stop others profiting free of charge from their time-consuming and costly efforts to find cures for cancer and other diseases.
Monti said the new text ruled out patents for animal or plant species or for cloning or genetic engineering involving human beings.

Parliament's large Socialist and Christian Democrat groups welcomed the Commission proposals, arguing that the EU's potentially lucrative biotechnological industry would continue to sink under competition from the United States and Japan unless its inventions were guaranteed clear EU-level protection.
Each of the EU's 15 countries has a different set of patent laws, hampering intra-European trade and creating legal uncertainty.

But critical Euro-MPs complained the proposal gave industry too much control over the "raw material of life", citing a growing number of U.S. patents for gene sequences -- the specific gene makeup -- and a patent granted to a U.S. company for procedures using blood cells from umbilical cords.
"This directive really leads to the privatisation of nature," said German Green Euro-MP Hildrud Breyer.

Parliament's development committee threatened to reject the proposal unless changes were made to ensure that developing countries, which supplied 83 percent of known genetic resources, were adequately compensated by pharmaceutical multinationals.
